records.name: North Gyeongsang
records.summary: The country dossier lists this division among regions with no sub-national trans signal: no province-specific trans ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding was located. This is an estimated record — its prior characterization as a conservative south-eastern province was model prior, not evidence, and is replaced here by the dossier's null finding. The same three national-level sources as other divisions in this country apply: a Seoul court ruling on police restroom advice, an unrestored Yonhap wire, and a national school-restroom survey — none document North Gyeongsang-specific incidents.

records.name: Jeju
records.summary:
No region-specific law, incident or enforcement finding about trans people exists in the audited record for this island, and the national framework applies: trans status is not criminalised; a May 2024 ruling removed surgical requirements for changing registered sex; and the July 2024 damages judgment against police advice that a transitioning person avoid public restrooms — with its appellate language on restroom use as a fundamental and universal human right — governs here as in the rest of the country. The same sources' national survey data (2021: large majorities of trans respondents reporting fear-driven facility avoidance) and a 2021 damages award for a student barred from academy restrooms describe the practical baseline.

An earlier characterisation of this island as the country's most permissive region was a model prior, not a finding; it is not supported by any surviving audited source and has been removed. What the record can support for a visitor is the national position on this island — lawful status, available courts, social ambivalence about facilities — and no locally documented fact making this island safer or harsher than that picture.

records.name: Sejong
records.summary:
The audited sources document no region-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding touching trans people in this administratively special city; what governs a visitor is the national framework: trans status is lawful; surgery cannot be required to amend registered sex after a May 2024 ruling; and in July 2024 a court awarded damages holding that police advice to a transitioning person to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, the appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right. The same record carries national survey data (2021) showing fear-driven restroom avoidance among trans respondents and a 2021 damages award for a student excluded from a private academy's facilities.

Whether the concentration of government agencies here changes official climate for trans residents or visitors is not documented in the audited record — neither protective nor hostile initiatives are recorded — so the city's visitor-facing facts reduce to the national framework and its documented social friction over public facilities.

records.name: Gwangju
records.summary:
For this city the audited record contains no local law, ordinance or incident series concerning trans people, and the national framework governs a visitor's exposure: trans status is not criminalised; legal gender recognition lost its surgical prerequisite in a May 2024 ruling; and in July 2024 a court held that police advice directing a transitioning person to avoid public restrooms was a personal-rights infringement, awarding damages after the appellate court described comfortable restroom use as a fundamental and universal human right. The attached national data — a 2021 survey of 591 trans respondents documenting fear-driven facility avoidance, and a 2021 damages award for a student barred from restrooms by a private academy — complete the baseline.

The prior reference to local Pride activity and a civic profile favourable to it has no support in the surviving audited sources and is withdrawn: the defensible statement is that the audited record documents nothing distinguishing this city from the national position, in protection or in hostility.

records.name: La Libertad
records.summary:
The Public Ministry's 2012–2021 study places La Libertad second in absolute LGTB-homicide count (10 of 88 — after Lima's 12, level with Lima Norte), centred on Trujillo. The region's population share (~3%) is far smaller than its death share (~11.4%), giving a per-capita lethality roughly 3.8× the national average — a materially concerning concentration not explained by population alone, and placing the unit below the national score (0.36).

Counterweight: Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR (regional session 3 September 2024, approved 6 September 2024, published in El Peruano November 2024) promotes labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people — their right to formal, dignified work in equitable conditions without discrimination on gender identity or expression, and recognition of the trans community as a vulnerable group. This is a resident-facing instrument (a visitor does not use it), but it evidences that this particular regional council legislated visibly for trans inclusion — the one such ordinance found in Peru's 26 departments. It also sits in the same department where rondas campesinas exercise recognised dispute-resolution authority, a structural caveat with no documented trans-specific case.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The per-capita violence concentration is the dominant factor; the ordinance prevents a larger deduction. vs Lima (now 0.38, above national): La Libertad's per-capita lethality remains worse, though Lima's higher absolute count and 2025 reporting case have lifted its score since the original comparison.

records.name: Tacna
records.summary:
On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of a hostel in central Tacna; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She had entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but, per the audited reporting, had not identified the suspect, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. On 23 May her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence.

The framework that reaches a visitor in Tacna in full: the audited reporting records that this country has neither a gender-identity law nor a hate-crime statute — so anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label marks investigative posture, not a charge — and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by reference to sexual orientation. Beyond this one incident and its response, no local ordinance, policing pattern against trans people, or municipal protection is documented; the investigating-as-hate-crime posture within a statute-less system is the audited local reality.

records.name: Atlántico
records.summary:
Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 annual report issues a specific, named warning of "increasing violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the Atlántico department," and quantifies it: 54 cases of intrafamily violence, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats and 8 lethal-violence cases in the department, with 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders; the report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories at "high" threat level. Barranquilla is the Caribbean-coast hub for trans sex work and the city where the NGO's documentation base operates, giving it both elevated exposure and visibility in monitoring data; the department appears explicitly in the 270-victim national total (+63% on 2024; one killing every 32 hours). Impunity is near-total nationally: 99.8% of threat cases never advanced past the investigation stage. A positive institutional signal is recorded: the department's development plan (and Barranquilla's) commits coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violent acts against LGBTIQ+ people.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Atlántico falls approximately 0.09 lower, justified by the NGO's named escalation warning (not merely inclusion in aggregate counts, but a specific "increase" call-out) and the structural role of Barranquilla's trans sex-work corridor. records.name: Bolívar
records.summary:
The murder of Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who campaigned with the "No Es Hora De Callar" movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of 500+ survivors of sexual violence, is documented in Bolívar on 22 May 2025; she was killed in Carmen de Bolívar, and more than 19 days after the killing the circumstances of what happened remain unclear (friend and fellow leader Yirley Velasco recalls her as a trans-rights fighter in the municipality). El Tiempo's data-journalism work on the gap between official Fiscalía and NGO (Caribe Afirmativo/Defensoría) figures names her case specifically. Bolívar appears within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged by Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 territorial-expansion finding, where state response is weakest.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Bolívar sits approximately 0.08 lower: the killing is a named, targeted murder of a community leader (not an undifferentiated count), and the department falls within the "territorial expansion" zone where the monitoring body documents insufficient state protection. Versus Antioquia (0.33), Bolívar is substantially higher because it carries one specific high-profile homicide rather than the 45-of-270 structural concentration and multi-case impunity pattern defining Antioquia. Versus Atlántico (0.43), Bolívar is marginally above: its evidence is a single named killing within an aggregate warning, whereas Atlántico carries a forward-looking escalation call-out tied to a larger trans sex-work hub.
